extracted.intended_audience: literate London readers of a periodical interested in manners, politics, and social commentary
extracted.subtask_short: periodical essay on manners and news
extracted.subtask_description: A periodical/essay combining social commentary (on courtship, duelling, characters, childrearing) with brief news items; aimed at instructing and entertaining early-18th-century readers about conduct and public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship: be a parrot, not a dove
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice for lovers: flatter and make your addresses before favour rather than remaining silent after obtaining it. (Original line: "For he who would be loved by women, must never be silent before the favour, or open his lips after it.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the parrot represents the lover in pursuit (flattering, voicing addresses), the dove the lover in possession. The essay argues "to be a parrot, is the only way to succeed; and to be a dove, to preserve your conquests." Anti-pattern: remaining silent until after favour (opening lips only after).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying a gentleman by person, habit, and trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Social classification can be inferred from appearance and possessions: the writer proposes to judge Jeffry Nicknack by seeing his person, habit, the shape of his snuff-box, and whether he takes 'Spanish or musty' snuff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test recommended: inspect a man's snuff-box and taste (Spanish vs musty) and his outfit to 'settle his character.' Implicit rule: outward trappings and fashionable consumables are valid signals of social type; absence of personal description leaves classification indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and signs of a 'smart fellow'
rubrics_metrics.description: Declares that calling a gentleman a 'smart fellow' is praise: 'a "smart fellow" is always an appellation of praise, and is a man of double capacity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs by which you may know a 'smart fellow': livelihood or education in the Civil List; a vivacity or mettle above his usual manner shown in a little jerk in motion, a short trip in his steps, well-fancied lining of his coat, or other indications of vigorous dress. Anti-pattern: taking offence at being called what your tailor and milliner have made you appear to be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of duelling as custom-driven folly, not honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Duelling is portrayed as arising from custom, fashion, and vanity rather than true courage or honour: it is called an 'illegitimate species of the ancient knight-errantry' and linked to mere affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments and examples offered: wise nations often avoid private fighting; mercenaries and paid bravado show courage tied to gain (not virtue); city militia rarely decide animosities by combat; anecdotes (Captain Crabtree/Maggot) show disputes are often farcical. Conclusion: duels are excessive adherence to custom, not marks of true sense or virtue; appeals to foreign examples (e.g., Venice) and satire of modern 'monsters' of chivalry support the critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and failings of critics and wits
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic is often the silliest because constant judgment makes him censorious and companionless; a wit is prone to premeditated jokes that do not arise from occasion and therefore lack true judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critic failings: inuring to examine everything makes him always passing sentence, earnest on trifles, and preventing him from being a companion. Wit failings: imagination without judgment leads to contrived turns; the wit invents occasions to display his sallies (example figures: Spondee the critic, Jasper Dactyle the wit). Recommended implication: genuine judgment and spontaneous appropriateness are virtues; premeditation and censoriousness are vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upbringing children: observe inclinations; cultivate thrift and providence
rubrics_metrics.description: On educating youth: study the temper and inclinations of childhood and youth to avoid giving vice and folly supplies from the growing generation; exhibit appropriate sights and cultivate provident habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical actions: take children to see the town's sights 'to sound their inclinations' but be mindful of corrupting entertainments; praise and keep the provident child (example: Jack who saves farthings) as promising a good husband, kind father, and honest executor. Implicit rule: matching instruction and exposure to the child's disposition and cultivating thrift are marks of wise rearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social honour and reputation measured by wealth and appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical social rule: honour and rank in the city are often determined by wealth and conspicuous appearance rather than true bravery—'the richest is the bravest man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and satire: promotions and ranks (captain to colonel, major) are said to follow financial shifts (fall of stocks, rising prices) rather than merit; 'you may measure a man's services by his waist, and the most prominent belly is certainly the man who has been most upon action.' Use as a critical lens on how public esteem is assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: On public political appeals and the limits of sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of rulers appealing to the people's assent: a sovereign's appeal to public opinion when acting without consent is misguided; people resist being governed without their consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by mock letter to the French king: admonishes that 'we were made for you, and not you for us' is false; subjects assert they will not wish success to a ruler acting against their interests and call for negotiation and consent. Implicit standard: legitimate rule requires consent and cannot safely rest on appeals to vanity or rhetoric.
